reason: 'Veins visible' means clearly visible. The accepted rules for evident, obvious, well-defined and well-marked all map to PATO:0000463 conspicuous. Negated forms ('not visible', 'invisible', 'scarcely visible') have their own rules to inconspicuous (R0067, R0173, R0136), so the negation worry does not arise.

For like parts that run together into one (sori, segments, lobes, appendages), FLOPO connate (like parts united by tissue fusion) fits, as with the accepted 'coalescent' rule. Confluent veins (anastomosing), spots and glands (colour or surface pattern) are not fusion of organs, so the rule should apply only to organ-type parts.

In floras 'delicate' means thin, slender, fine, tender or easily damaged, depending on the part. PATO fragile is a disposition to break and covers only one of these readings. No single existing class fits, so the word should stay unmapped.

PATO:0001786 split (divided into parts) has 'septate' as an explicit NARROW synonym in ont/quality.obo. PO:0000030 septum (used by rule R0445) only covers partitions of cavities formed by fused organs, so it would not fit septate hairs. Split is the existing class that covers all the uses.

In PATO, involute (0001962), revolute (0001963) and convolute (0001966) are all subclasses of curled (0000405). Bare 'rolled' does not give the direction, so the parent class is the correct, safe mapping.

'Rooting' (at the nodes, at the tips) means roots arising from the shoot system, which is PO:0000042 shoot-borne root. That holds for stems, stolons, nodes and also fronds and leaf tips (walking ferns). It should not apply when the bearer is a root.
'Veins apparent' means clearly visible, the same reading as 'evident' (C323). The opposite, 'not apparent', is already mapped to inconspicuous (R0526), so the pair stays consistent.

French 'mat' (English 'matt') means not shiny, which is FLOPO:0991106 dull, but the English noun 'mat' means mat-forming (FLOPO:0991010). Limiting the rule to surface-bearing parts avoids catching the noun on a whole plant.

When said of plants, 'gregarious' means growing in groups, which fits PATO aggregated (clumped, clustered). 'Gregarious flowering' (synchronised mass flowering) is a different meaning, so the rule should apply only to whole-plant bearers.

PATO multi-colored is defined as 'two or more hues', so bicolored is a correct (if broader) mapping and no bicolored class exists. This matches the accepted rule R0552 'bicoloured'. For leaves with two differently coloured faces, FLOPO discolorous is more exact.

Heteromorphic means occurring in different forms, not necessarily two. The accepted rule R0102 maps 'polymorphic' to PATO variant shape, with FLOPO dimorphic as the narrower two-form case. Mapping to dimorphic would claim exactly two forms where the text does not say so.

Epigeal stems, stolons and cotyledons are above the ground, which is FLOPO aerial; the accepted 'epigeous' rule (R0569) gives the same reading. 'Germination epigeal' with a seed or seedling as bearer is a germination type, not a position, so it must be excluded.
FLOPO:0991051 villous is defined as 'bearing long, soft, shaggy hairs', so shaggy is covered by the definition itself. 'Shaggy bark' (exfoliating) is the only misfit and is rare among the examples.

'Ample' panicles, sheaths and blades are large, which is PATO increased size (relatively high size; synonyms big, enlarged). The examples include panicles and sheaths, so the organ list proposed by the first check is too narrow.
'Cracked' is already a listed synonym of FLOPO:0991022 fissured, whose definition covers bark, other surfaces and axes. It matches the accepted rules for 'cracking' (R0366) and 'rimose' (R0619).

'Widening distally' describes a part that becomes wider along its length, which is the shape PATO dilated describes, not a process. It matches the accepted rules 'expanding' (R0508), 'ampliate' (R0225) and 'expanded' (C181).
Corrugate surfaces are thrown into wrinkles or folds, which is PATO rugose. The accepted rules 'corrugated' (R0097), 'puckered' (R0262) and 'rugulate' (R0660) all use the same class.

'Veins not visible' means not clearly visible. The accepted rules for invisible, hardly visible, barely visible, imperceptible, obscure and indistinct all map to PATO:0000464 inconspicuous. Relational uses ('not visible through the utricle') go to pattern 09.

config/botanical_colour_synonyms.tsv (ISCC-NBS based) already maps buff and all its compounds (pale buff, grayish buff and others) to PATO:0104054 orange yellow. Changing only this rule would make the colour mapping inconsistent. PATO beige could be considered if the colour table itself is revised.

PATO:0002256 tricuspidate (having three cusps) is the existing term for an apex with three teeth or points; there is no tridentate class. Using a count of three teeth (pattern 03) is the only other option, and a rule to an existing term is preferred.

'Connective produced beyond the thecae' and 'rachilla produced' fit FLOPO excurrent (extending beyond the apex of the structure it runs through). 'Leaf produced into a tip' or 'base produced into a spur' do not fit, so the rule should apply only to axial parts that run through a structure.
The definition of FLOPO:0991175 cauliflorous covers flowers arising 'from the trunk or from older, leafless woody branches', so ramiflory falls inside it.

PATO:0001950 blunt is defined as 'terminating gradually in a rounded end', which describes a narrowly rounded apex. Plain 'rounded' maps to obtuse, but 'narrowly' points to the gradual rounded tip that blunt describes.
This is pubescent plus a degree word. The playbook drops degree modifiers and keeps them as a cue in the record (as with 'longitudinally fissured'), and there is no 'sparsely pubescent' class.

PATO terminal means located at an end. Apical pores, anthers, inflorescences and apical hairs on a leaf are all at the end of the part that bears them. 'Apical or subapical' pairs with PATO subterminal. The first check's restriction would exclude correct uses such as anther pores.

Aggregate spikes and pseudobulbs are clustered, which is PATO aggregated. 'Aggregate fruit' names a part (PO:0025628 aggregate fruit) and should change the bearer, not become a quality, so fruit must be excluded.

Erect-spreading means directed obliquely upward, between erect and spreading. The accepted rule R0499 maps the same word 'erect-patent' to PATO ascending, which is defined as directed upward at an oblique angle. Semi erect is a kind of erect and is vaguer.

Stems, stolons and nodes that are rooted bear shoot-borne roots (PO:0000042). For a whole plant ('deeply rooted'), 'rooted' refers to the main root system, not shoot-borne roots, and for a root bearer it makes no sense.
Echinulate means minutely echinate, and echinate is already mapped to PATO:0001365 spiny (C306). No diminutive class exists, so the broader existing term is preferred over a new one.
Sclerified endocarps, perigone segments and roots are hardened by thick-walled cells. The accepted rules for indurate (C305), sclerotic (R0546), horny and corneous all map to PATO:0000386 hard.
